evidence.title: A National Cross-Sectional Survey of Artificial Intelligence Patient Safety Reporting Infrastructure Available to US Nurses
evidence.outcome: Availability of formal channels for nurses to report AI-related patient safety concerns
evidence.effect: Of 424 nurses who encountered an AI safety concern, 83 (19.6%) reported no formal channel; non-hospital nurses had higher odds of no channel (OR 2.54; 95% CI 1.54-4.19).
evidence.quote: Among 424 nurses who encountered an AI-related patient safety concern, 83 (19.6%) reported no formal channel for reporting it.

commentary.bottom_line: One uncontrolled pre-post study tested an AI feedback pathway, and it received no patient complaints in five months, which cannot distinguish absent harms from unused channels. Two hazard studies suggest that reporting channels are often missing and that voluntary feedback declines as use grows, but no study tested training or non-retaliation protections.

perspectives.view: A single pre-post study without a comparator (64 evaluations of 55 AI solutions) tested the practice and found zero patient complaints over five months. The design, the absence of a control, and an outcome that cannot separate true absence of harm from non-use support very low certainty. User training and non-retaliation components have no direct tests.

Of 424 nurses who met an AI safety concern, 83 (19.6%) reported no formal channel. Harms that go unreported cannot be traced or corrected. Whether adding a channel raises detection of errors before they reach patients remains untested, and the one test produced no reports to assess.

In one hospital, voluntary feedback fell after a 28-physician pilot as routine use expanded to 1,028 users and 14,910 conversations. This suggests that passive reporting channels may lose fidelity at scale, and the authors concluded that automated monitoring may be needed alongside user reports.

Non-hospital nurses had higher odds of lacking any reporting channel (OR 2.54; 95% CI 1.54-4.19). Care settings outside hospitals may therefore carry larger reporting gaps. No study examined whether patients with limited English proficiency or low literacy can use AI feedback channels.

Utah HB 452 requires mental health chatbot operators to document actions taken to mitigate harmful interactions, and FDA draft guidance encourages users to report device issues within 48 hours. NIST AI 600-1 and several European sources call for feedback processes. None of these sources cites outcome evidence that reporting channels reduce harm.

One site added AI feedback to existing patient feedback systems, which suggests the channel can be built on current infrastructure at modest cost. The pathway produced no complaints in five months. Separately, falling voluntary feedback at scale suggests staff time spent on channels may yield diminishing returns without automated monitoring.

Zero patient complaints in five months may reflect that patients did not know the pathway existed or did not recognize AI involvement in their care. The study did not report patient awareness. Patients cannot report an AI error they cannot see, so disclosure of AI use may be a precondition for this safeguard.

commentary.research_gap: Controlled studies should compare report volume, report quality, and time to error correction between sites with and without AI reporting channels. These studies should test user training and non-retaliation protections as separate components, and they should measure staff and patient awareness of the channel so that low report counts can be interpreted.
commentary.underserved_note: No study, including the single test of the practice, reported enrolling or analyzing Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. The nurse survey found larger channel gaps outside hospitals. Health systems serving these groups have no evidence on whether standard feedback channels reach their patients and may need to evaluate language access and plain-language design locally.
